parent.name: English Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...b6 (or 1...e6 2.c4 b6) intending ...Bb7, a hypermodern set-up in which the bishop on b7 pressures e4 and the centre rather than occupying it. After 3.e4 Bb7 White builds a broad pawn centre (Bd3, f3, Nc3) and Black undermines it with ...Bb4(+), ...f5 and sometimes ...Qh4, as in Polugaevsky-Korchnoi 1977 (4.Qc2 Qh4 5.Nd2 Bb4). The play is double-edged: Black gives White space and a strong centre, then goes for counterplay and tactics against it. Gambit versions (Hartlaub 4...f5, Polli 4.f3 f5) and 3.Nc3 Bb4 transpositions to a ...b6 Nimzo-Indian are the main branches. It was a surprise weapon of Speelman, Short, Miles and Keene in the 1980s and is rare in elite play, although some club players use 1...b6/2...Bb7 as a universal system.

parent.name: Bird Opening
parent.overview: 1.f4 stakes a claim to e5 and gives White attacking chances at the cost of slightly weakening the kingside (the h4-e1 diagonal). Black's most common reply is 1...d5, which gives a reversed Dutch Defence with White a tempo up, and White chooses between a reversed Leningrad (Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O), a Stonewall (pawns on d4, e3, f4, with a kingside pawn storm) or a queenside fianchetto to hold e5. Black's sharpest answer is 1...e5, From's Gambit, which is notoriously double-edged and shows the Qh4+ danger. Other replies include 1...Nf6, 1...c5 and 1...b6. White scores below 50% (about 47%), and the opening is rare at the very top, but it is a respectable surprise weapon (Larsen, Bird).

parent.name: English Opening: King's English Variation
parent.overview: After 1.c4 e5 White has what is in effect a Sicilian Defence with colours reversed and an extra tempo (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads with very different set-ups: the Botvinnik System (c4, Nc3, g3, Bg2, d3, e4, Nge2) is a slow bind on d5; the Four Knights (2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6) and 3.g3 lines give fianchetto systems; the Flohr-Mikenas-type 3.e4 and 2.Nc3 Nf6 with an early d4 are sharper (s1, s2, s4). White's recurring themes are control of d5, queenside expansion with b4 and Rb1, and the long diagonal (s2, s4). Black neutralises the extra tempo with ...d5 breaks, ...f5 or an early ...Bb4 (s2). Overall the play is flexible and manoeuvring with little forcing theory (s1, s2), though the Four Knights in this move order is described as sharper than its 1.e4 cousin (s4).

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Modern Variations
parent.overview: 2...d6 is a crossroads, not a single set-up. It is the move order that leads to the Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen and Classical/Richter-Rauzer after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 (s4). The open Sicilian is open and extremely complex: White has a lead in development and extra kingside space, Black has a central pawn majority and the open c-file (s1). White often castles queenside against Black's queenside counterplay, giving opposite-side attacks (Yugoslav Attack, English Attack) (s1). 2...d6 also keeps ...d5 off for a move, which is why White has quieter tries here: 3.Bc4, 3.Nc3 and 3.d3 or the Alapin-like 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3 (Tartakower, in the subtree) (s3). The root is described as combative and unbalanced (s2), but how sharp a game is depends heavily on whether White plays 3.d4 or an anti-Sicilian.

parent.name: English Opening: Agincourt Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.c4 with ...e6, preparing ...d5 with full support and keeping nearly every queen-pawn set-up available. The opening is a transposition magnet: 2.Nc3 d5 gives a QGD-like structure, 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 a Catalan or Reti, 2.d4 c5 an Anglo-Indian or Queen's Pawn-type game, and 2.e4 a French-like game. Black can also choose Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Indian set-ups after ...Nf6. Play is described as calm, positional and non-forcing; the c8-bishop's development is Black's main early question. Master usage is spread among specialists (Miezis, Uhlmann, Korchnoi, Flear, Sveshnikov, Rozentalis) rather than concentrated, and it is a normal solid choice at every level.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. Qe2
parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.
